codex.worst_flaw: The reward can credit checklists submitted before technicians inspect the site, and the audit specifies no reliable way to detect those sign-offs, leaving a safety risk that should block launch.

claude.worst_flaw: Credit is based on the checklist being submitted before work starts, and there is no in-field check that the inspection actually happened, such as photo, geolocation or time-on-site evidence. A 10-a-week desk review of records cannot reliably catch someone tapping through the form before seeing the site, and the team completion rate shown in the crew channel could create peer pressure on small crews where individuals can be identified.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, paid time, privacy limits, quality sampling, safety-hold credit and a staggered pilot with workflow fixes make it approvable, but a 30-minute reward and a private-thanks announcement may give limited visibility and pull, and lasting change depends on the workflow fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The optional two-week crew comparison lacks an assignment rule and a plan to account for differences in jobs, leaving the reward’s incremental effect uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning plan compares groups over only a two-week staggered window and does not address sample size or uncertainty. The quality audit samples just five credited jobs a week across a 300-person workforce. Together, these give weak evidence on whether the reward added value and whether checks were rushed.

holistic.reason: Co-designed with stewards, fixes app friction first, rewards the completed check rather than the outcome, protects hazard reporting and keeps scores private under the union agreement, but its measurement rules are complex and a one-hour group reward is modest, so it is not obvious the habit will stick once the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design is a single before-and-after comparison with no comparison crews or plain-support arm, so any rise above 35% cannot be credited to the meal reward rather than the offline fixes, paid practice or prefilled workflow. On top of that, the 80% crew threshold that applies only in weeks 5 and 6 is not tied to the 35% baseline, which makes the reward an all-or-nothing group stake that could push crews to pressure each other.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a plain-feedback comparison group, the pilot cannot tell whether the crew reward improves pre-job checklist completion beyond the app fixes, paid practice, and workflow prompt.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a shared crew-level reward, no penalties, privacy protections, safety-first handling of hazards, and a verified measurement rule make it approvable, but a 30-minute meal break is a modest incentive, so visibility and durable habit depend on the workflow fix made before the reward ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design is only a before/after comparison against a recalculated four-week baseline. It has no comparison arm, so it cannot separate the reward from the queue and review-block fixes, and it gives no uncertainty or harm outcomes such as defect escapes or reviewer load.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the lunch reward alongside the shared queue and protected reviewer coverage, so any improvement leaves the reward’s incremental value unknown.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with baseline, anti-gaming checks, team-level reward and a fix-the-bottleneck-first approach that suits sceptical engineers, but it is administratively heavy and the 85% on-time target and lunch reward are modest motivators, so durability rests mostly on the workflow changes rather than the incentive.

codex.worst_flaw: The trial introduces the reward alongside queue and staffing changes, and the later withdrawal period cannot reliably distinguish the reward’s effect from carryover or changes in workload.

claude.worst_flaw: The design measures the reward only by comparing before and after, with no plain-support comparison or check for spillover and case mix, so it cannot show whether the paid-time-off reward adds anything beyond the queue and coverage fixes made at the same time.

holistic.reason: The proposal fixes the queue before any reward, pays out a team-wide time-off reward, uses an audited and gaming-resistant metric with no rankings, and keeps the default queue and coverage afterwards, though its complexity, the 85% threshold and the fading reward lower the odds of lasting change.

claude.worst_flaw: The design learns only from a before/after comparison with a four-week baseline and has no comparison group or isolation of the reward's effect beyond the blocker fix and workflow changes, so the keep/change/drop decision cannot tell what actually caused any improvement.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside workflow fixes and private feedback, so it cannot establish whether the paid half-day improves review turnaround beyond what those supports achieve on their own.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with a clear metric, anti-gaming safeguards, privacy protections and a diagnosis step, but a team-wide threshold with a half-day reward is a modest hook, relies on a captain's weekly sampling effort, and the one-time reward plus end-of-pilot checks leave durability dependent on the workflow fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The meal depends on a single monthly observer audit, and without a plain-feedback comparison or a way to account for sampling uncertainty and case mix, the pilot cannot establish whether the reward improved hand hygiene.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never compares the three wards against an untreated comparison or plain-support condition, and it uses no uncertainty bounds on small monthly observer samples, so it cannot tell whether a 5-point change comes from the meal, the workflow fixes, Hawthorne effects or audit noise. Its Keep/Change/Drop decisions rest on single-ward before/after readings.

holistic.reason: Safety-conscious and well-governed with audited outcomes, ward-level reward, and clear stop rules, but the meal is a modest, delayed incentive tied to a single audit and the complexity of tracking and rules may blunt staff attention and durable habit change.

codex.worst_flaw: The kiosk rollout can pass on audited hand-hygiene compliance alone, even if nurses log very few of the hand-hygiene moments they complete.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design has no comparison or control: it uses a pre/post change in the monthly Hawthorne-prone observer audit across three wards, with no isolation from plain workflow fixes, no seasonal or case-mix adjustment, no sample-size reasoning and no event or policy versioning or appeal path.

holistic.reason: The proposal rewards audited outcomes rather than kiosk volume, fixes workflow first, has pause and sample-size safeguards and avoids individual tracking, but a one-time team meal is a weak, easily overlooked motivator and the habit has little to carry it three months after the pilot ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison ward or other control, and no predefined analysis of uncertainty, so it cannot tell whether a change in logging or compliance came from the reward or from plain workflow fixes and secular trends. Ward-level targets also ignore case mix and uneven opportunity volume, the reward rests on monthly observer samples without a minimum sample size or a confidence rule, and the event history has no replayable versioning or formal appeals.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the design defines when unverifiable actions invalidate the score, since a selectively verifiable sample can qualify a ward for the reward even when its actual logging rate falls below 80%.

holistic.reason: Safety-first design with independent audit, tight gaming controls, and a sensible kiosk-default fade-out, but a monthly team meal reward is low-salience, 12-week wins rely on workflow habits rather than internal motivation, and audit sampling constraints could make logging verification fragile.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward and the one-click linking workflow overlap during the scored milestone, so the pilot cannot tell whether paid time off adds value beyond workflow support and private feedback.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never compares the rally against plain workflow support or a comparison group, so the pre/post coverage thresholds can't tell whether the reward added value beyond the tooling fixes and seasonal case mix, and CSAT bonus interaction with resolution speed is only watched, not tested.

holistic.reason: Well-designed team-wide reward with quality checks, CSAT protection, protected time and a data-driven post-rally decision rule, though a single paid hour is a modest motivator and 6 weeks of rally may fade without the workflow fixes sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot changes the workflow during the reward period and has no plain-feedback comparison group, so it cannot determine whether paid time off adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The design learns from one before-and-after coverage number with no comparison group and no quality measure after payout, so it cannot tell whether the rally or the easier workflow changed anything, and in-rally gaming could pass as success.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with baseline checks, quality sampling, CSAT guardrails and a keep/change/drop decision, but a single hour of time off at 50% coverage (from 12%) may feel distant, and the team-level threshold risks weak individual salience.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a comparison group receiving the same workflow support and private feedback without the reward, the pilot cannot determine whether paid time off improves adoption, especially because article suggestions move to the front of the resolution panel during the reward qualification window.

claude.worst_flaw: There is no concurrent comparison group or plain-support arm, so the pilot cannot separate the incentive's effect from the workflow fixes and the new resolution-panel UI. The 30%/baseline decision bands therefore rest on an uncontrolled before/after measure.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with a clear single rule, fixed blockers, private goals, quality sampling, and CSAT guardrails, but the one-hour team reward is weak, the weekly team-rate post is low-salience, and extrinsic incentives rarely sustain the habit unless the workflow friction fixes carry it.
